extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners (applicants and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications for compliance with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph). Covers principles, case law, examiner burden, and procedural steps for assessing whether the specification demonstrates possession of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement (separate from enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 require that 'the specification shall contain a written description of the invention ....' This requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: (1) to clearly convey the information that an applicant has invented the subject matter claimed and (2) to convey to the public what the applicant claims as the invention. The requirement 'implements the principle that a patent must describe the technology that is sought to be patented' and 'serves both to satisfy the inventor’s obligation to disclose the technologic knowledge ... and to demonstrate that the patentee was in possession of the invention that is claimed.' (Cited case law: Ariad, Vas‑Cath, Univ. of Rochester, Capon, In re Curtis, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail (possession standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession is required but possession alone does not cure lack of written description. Compliance is a fact‑based inquiry varying with the nature of the invention. (Cited cases: Moba, Vas‑Cath, Enzo Biochem.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to show possession (descriptive means)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant shows possession by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using descriptive means such as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice, by showing that the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., drawings or structural chemical formulas showing the invention was complete), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. (Cited: Lockwood; Pfaff; Amgen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological material deposits do not substitute for written description
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposit of biological material (in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.) may satisfy written description for a claimed material but is not a substitute for a written description of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written description of the deposited material needs to be as complete as possible because examination proceeds solely on the basis of the written description. Deposits made after filing may support sequence corrections only if applicant files a conforming 37 CFR 1.804 statement. (Cited: Enzo Biochem; In re Lundak; 54 Fed. Reg. final rule.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of adequate written description for original claims (but not absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; the PTO has the initial burden of presenting reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as describing the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even original claims may raise written description issues if an aspect of the claimed invention is not described with sufficient particularity (e.g., claims embracing additional structures beyond a disclosed sequence). Examine specification and drawings to assess support for originally filed claims. (Cited: In re Wertheim.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Function‑only or method‑of‑making descriptions may not show possession of product structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing an invention solely in terms of a method of making and/or its function may lack written descriptive support for the structure responsible for the function when there is no described or art‑recognized correlation between the function and the structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: amino acid sequence plus genetic code might not place inventor in possession of naturally occurring DNA/mRNA encoding the protein. A description that merely renders the invention obvious may not be sufficient. (Cited: In re Bell; In re Deuel; Eli Lilly.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus/species and breadth support (genus disclosure may not support all species)
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic or 'laundry list' disclosure does not necessarily provide written description support for every species within a genus unless the disclosure reasonably leads those skilled in the art to the particular species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ordinary artisan must be able to 'envisage' the claimed product arising from the disclosed process; mere listing of possible moieties may be insufficient. Cases: Fujikawa; In re Ruschig; Purdue Pharma. Use caution when claiming broad ranges or subgenera without specific support.

rubrics_metrics.name: New or amended claims must be supported by the original disclosure (no new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition against introducing new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251) prevents adding information beyond originally filed subject matter; new or amended claims that introduce elements or limitations not supported by the original disclosure violate the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support may be express, implicit, or inherent; no in haec verba requirement. Amendments correcting obvious errors may be permissible if the ordinary artisan would recognize the error and appropriate correction. For sequence corrections, deposits and 37 CFR 1.804 statements can affect permissibility. (Cited: In re Rasmussen; In re Lukach; In re Smith; In re Oda; Cubist v. Hospira.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element described as essential raises written description issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that omits matter the applicant describes as essential or critical in the specification may fail the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where specification statements make clear that a particular (narrow) understanding is essential, broader claims omitting that element may be invalid. Such omissions may also raise enablement or definiteness problems. (Cited: PIN/NIP v. Platte Chem.; Gentry Gallery; Tronzo.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must make a prima facie case identifying unsupported claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a prima facie case of lack of written description, the examiner must identify the claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hyatt v. Dudas — examiner explained lack of adequate description of a claimed combination despite individual elements being listed. Once the examiner makes a prima facie case, the burden shifts to applicant to point out support or amend. For newly added/amended claims, a simple statement noting lack of apparent support for a given limitation may suffice to start the examination discussion. (Cited: Hyatt; Stored Value Solutions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers (claim construction component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is essential: each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the entire claim including preamble language and the transitional phrase ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of'). Guidance on open/closed claim language and when 'consisting essentially of' may be treated as 'comprising' for prior art purposes. Evaluate whether preamble language is structural or limiting (Pac‑Tec; Bell Communications Research; Corning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate sufficiency of recited structures, acts, or functions; do not import limitations from the specification into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should evaluate whether sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim; limitations may not be imported into the claims from the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of definitions or details for well‑established terms or procedures should not alone justify a written description rejection. Consider weight of preamble and whether claim limitations provide clear scope. (Cited: Lockwood; Bell Communications Research.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Review entire application to understand how applicant provides support for claimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess support by reviewing the whole application: specification, drawings, originally filed claims, examples, and any deposits or cross‑references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support for originally filed claims may be found in any portion of the specification or drawings. Examiner should also consider whether corrections, incorporations by reference, or inherent disclosures provide support; examination is fact‑specific and depends on the level of ordinary skill and predictability of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant obligations when amending claims — point out original support
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant amends claims, applicant should specifically point out where and/or how the original disclosure supports the amendment(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant points to support and the examiner finds the disclosure does not reasonably convey possession, the examiner must present reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize such support. A simple statement pointing out lack of apparent support for a limitation may be sufficient to trigger further explanation by the examiner. (Cited: MPEP §§ 2163.04, 714.02.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description inquiry is fact‑based and depends on the nature of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the written description requirement is met is a question of fact determined case‑by‑case and will 'necessarily vary depending on the nature of the invention claimed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consider predictability of the art, level of ordinary skill, examples and working embodiments, and whether the disclosure imparts sufficient knowledge to those skilled in the art about the claimed subject matter. (Cited: Enzo Biochem; In re Smith; In re Wertheim.)
